learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected about 36% and locked the largest-group prediction after doubling random friendships from 100 to 200 among 200 people.
observations.exploration: Tested all density choices in order. Biggest groups were 9 at 0.5 average friends, 36 at 1.0, 76 at 1.25, 110 at 1.5, 148 at 2.0 and 183 at 3.0. Second group shrank from 23 at 1.25 to three at 2.0.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the answer to about 75%, accurately listed every visited density and group size, and explained that links can merge already large groups. It disclosed one invented random crowd rather than a real network measurement.
observations.visual: Inspected the inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshot at density two. Most nodes and edges were gold for the 148-person component, while a tiny green component represented the second largest. The tangled edge picture required the numeric readouts to quantify it.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884163 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The question challenges proportional scaling of a connected structure.

interaction.reason: Density choices expose rapid merging across a transition and contrast the second group.
interaction.evidence: Biggest share reached 74% at density two while the runner-up had only three nodes.

payoff.reason: The reveal accurately uses all explored cases and gives a merging mechanism.
payoff.evidence: It names the full sequence and distinguishes invented random links from real data.

clarity.reason: Colors and counts distinguish a dominant component despite edge clutter.
clarity.evidence: Gold largest and green second components have explicit sizes.

transfer.reason: The connectivity principle is explained without a new network application.
transfer.evidence: Only one fixed crowd and link realization are tested.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: Doubling links more than quadruples the biggest group's share.
surprise.evidence: The largest component grows from 36 to 148 people.

visualExplanation.reason: Coloring reveals dominance, but the dense edge drawing obscures individual mergers.
visualExplanation.evidence: The two-connection screenshot is a tangled gold network.

playfulness.reason: Density choices invite watching components merge.
playfulness.evidence: Six stages span sparse groups to a nearly connected crowd.

practicalValue.reason: It gives intuition for network connectivity thresholds.
practicalValue.evidence: The reveal explains why new links can combine entire groups.

depth.reason: The second-largest group adds evidence beyond a rising maximum.
depth.evidence: Its size falls as one dominant group absorbs others.

complexity.reason: Simple buttons control a graph, while indirect connectivity and nonlinear merging require a new abstraction.
complexity.conceptualDemand: Moderate: track connected groups rather than individual friend counts.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: One new link can combine two entire components.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: Connected components and random network transitions are introduced.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: Moderate: a dense node-link view and average-degree readouts.

whyCool: A modest number of extra friendships can suddenly connect most people through chains of acquaintances.
caveat: The toy uses one made-up crowd with random links and no fresh seed control.
missingEvidence: No new network or application was tested.
